title: Yjs vs Automerge: Which CRDT Should You Use for Your Real-Time Collaboration App?
query: I'm building a real-time collaboration app and need to choose between Yjs and Automerge for CRDTs. Which one should I use? Do a deep dive.
scope_constraints: JavaScript/TypeScript ecosystem implied (both libraries primarily target JS/TS)
No specific constraints on budget, team size, or platform
summary: For most real-time collaboration apps, Yjs is the recommended CRDT choice due to its superior performance (2-5x faster across benchmarks), dramatically smaller bundle size (20KB vs 604KB gzipped), vastly larger ecosystem (22k stars, 20M+ npm downloads/month), and broader editor support. Automerge 3.0 has made impressive strides in memory efficiency (10x reduction) and offers a cleaner batteries-included experience via automerge-repo with built-in version control APIs, but Yjs's performance lead, production track record (Evernote, Linear, ProtonMail, Typst, etc.), and massive community make it the safer default.

findings.claim: Yjs is consistently 2-5x faster than Automerge across standard collaborative editing benchmarks, with significantly smaller update messages (27 bytes vs 121 bytes per operation)

Yjs has vastly greater community adoption: 22k GitHub stars vs 6.3k, 20.5M monthly npm downloads vs 146k, and a much broader roster of production users (Evernote, GitBook, Linear, ProtonMail Docs, Typst, AFFiNE)
Automerge 3.0 achieved a ~10x memory reduction, making documents with long histories practical (Moby Dick: 700MB to 1.3MB)
Yjs has broader editor integration (15+ editors) compared to Automerge (ProseMirror only via community cookbook)
Automerge's automerge-repo provides a more polished batteries-included developer experience with built-in version control APIs (diff, history, view) that Yjs lacks natively
Both libraries are MIT-licensed, network-agnostic, support offline editing, and are suitable for local-first architecture

risks: Benchmark recency: Primary CRDT benchmarks tested Yjs 13.6.11 against Automerge 2.1.10; Automerge 3.0 was released after these benchmarks and may narrow the performance gap
Potential bias: The crdt-benchmarks repository is maintained by Kevin Jahns, the creator of Yjs. While benchmarks are open-source and reproducible, this is a potential conflict of interest
Automerge 3.0 is recent (July 2025); long-term production reliability data for this version is limited
Benchmarks primarily measure local operation processing; real-world performance under network latency and concurrent multi-user editing may differ
Yjs's B4x100 benchmark (608,908ms for 26M operations) suggests even Yjs struggles with extremely large documents
Automerge's smaller community means fewer third-party integrations and higher risk of project abandonment
Evaluation focuses on text-editing collaboration; trade-offs may differ for non-text use cases (canvas, whiteboard, structured data)
No independent third-party benchmarks were found; results rely on Yjs-author-maintained benchmarks
recommendations: Use Yjs if building a production collaboration app now — it offers the broadest editor support, best performance, largest ecosystem, and most battle-tested reliability
Use Automerge if prioritizing built-in version control (diff, history, branching), a cleaner batteries-included DX, or building on Rust/Swift natively
Consider hybrid approaches using Yjs with managed services like Liveblocks, Y-Sweet, or Hocuspocus for backend infrastructure
If memory or bundle size is critical, Yjs's 20KB gzipped bundle makes it the clear winner for web applications
If needing native mobile (Swift/Rust), Automerge's official Swift bindings and Rust core may be more straightforward
Prototype with both before committing — Automerge's trajectory of rapid improvement may continue to narrow the gap
